subject: chemistry
title: Igneous, Sedimentary, Metamorphic
welcome_lead: Three rock families with three different birth stories. Let's meet them.
meta_desc: Compare igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks in this KS3 chemistry adventure.
final_note: You can now identify any rock by how it was formed.

concepts.def: Formed when magma or lava cools and solidifies.
Formed from layers of sediment compressed over time.
Formed when existing rock is changed by heat and pressure.
Small particles like sand, mud, or shells.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Igneous rocks form when magma (underground) or lava (above ground) cools and hardens.

Slow cooling → big crystals (granite). Fast cooling → tiny crystals (basalt).

Sedimentary rocks form from layers of sediment that pile up at the bottom of seas or lakes. Over millions of years, they get pressed and cemented together.

Sandstone, limestone, chalk.

Metamorphic rocks form when other rocks are squeezed and heated deep underground. They don't melt — they recrystallise.

Limestone → marble. Mud → slate.

mcqs.q: If a reaction has a negative Gibbs free energy change, what does that mean?
options: A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
A reaction with negative delta G will always happen quickly.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
The reaction is thermodynamically feasible — it can proceed — but it may still be very slow.

mcqs.q: How is a dynamic equilibrium different from a static one?
options: Dynamic and static equilibria are the same thing because both show constant macroscopic properties.
A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
In a dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; in a static equilibrium, nothing is happening at the particle level.
A dynamic equilibrium means the system is still changing visibly.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
options: A strong acid is one that has been heated to higher temperature.
Strong and concentrated mean the same thing for acids.
A strong acid fully dissociates in water; a concentrated acid has a high amount of acid per volume — these are independent properties.
A reaction with negative delta G must be exothermic in every case.
